title: Enduro Race — lessons from using AI assistance to build and tune a browser motorcycle physics game
author: Usual-Advisor-7478
selftext:
I have been developing Enduro Race, a free 2D motorcycle game that runs directly in desktop and mobile browsers. The player balances the bike across hills, rocks, logs and wooden obstacles, tries to improve level times, collects coins, unlocks motorcycles and upgrades their performance.



Generative AI was used as an assistant across graphics, sound, text and code, and that use is disclosed on the [itch.io](http://itch.io) page. I remained hands-on with the game design, requirements, testing, integration and repeated tuning. The hardest part was not producing an initial prototype; it was making the visible game and the physics agree consistently. I spent many iterations checking terrain curves, rock and obstacle collision shapes, the lower silhouette of the motorcycle, mobile balance response, saved progression and performance during longer mobile sessions.



The process taught me that AI output still needs strict visual testing and small, isolated changes. When several systems were changed together, regressions became much harder to identify. Returning to clean versions, comparing the rendered shape with the physical body and testing desktop and mobile separately produced much better results.



Playable build: [https://danigame1.itch.io/enduro-race](https://danigame1.itch.io/enduro-race)



I would be interested to hear how other developers structure AI-assisted iteration when a game mixes visual assets, custom physics and two control schemes. What verification methods have helped you prevent a visual change from drifting away from its collision model?
